source.title: Laplacian smoothing gradient descent
source.authors: S. Osher; Bao Wang; Peng-Hang Yin; Xiyang Luo; Farzin Barekat; Minh Pham; A. Lin

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied; it includes some apparent OCR or transcription errors, but the relevant results are readable.
record.tranche_reason: Tests a new gradient-smoothing optimizer on natural-label classification and reports held-out performance, extending optimizer and batch-size findings to this method.
record.gate_note: The paper reports generalization results for Laplacian-smoothed SGD and RMSProp. It does not test random-label memorization, width, convolutional versus fully connected architectures, dropout, magnitude-aware sharpness, or removal of memorized examples. The LeNet batch-size discussion covers small batches, not the large-batch penalty in V5.
record.test_reason: The study tests Laplacian gradient smoothing, but none of V1–V8. It does not compare adaptive optimizers against SGD on held-out benchmarks, test a large-batch penalty, or measure magnitude-aware sharpness and generalization gaps. Reporting improved generalization for a new optimizer alone does not test these versions.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that Laplacian smoothing reduces gradient variance and optimality gaps, permits larger steps, and improves their numerical examples. They also identify adaptive selection of the smoothing parameter as unresolved. Their explanation of ResNet generalization through flatter minima remains a conjecture.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a Laplacian-smoothed gradient transformation, sometimes combined with SGD or RMSProp; it does not test the original interventions in the listed claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcome varies with batch size for LeNet-5; WGAN sample-quality gains are less pronounced at the smaller generator learning rate. The paper also says smoothing the critic showed no clear quality improvement.

fits_no_version.finding: First- and second-order Laplacian smoothing improve average MNIST logistic-regression test accuracy by more than 1% relative to SGD.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Laplacian gradient smoothing can improve held-out accuracy in subset-trained MNIST logistic regression.

fits_no_version.finding: LS-SGD maintains accuracy above 99.4% across tested LeNet batch sizes; SGD reaches 97% at batch size 4 and random-guess performance at batch size 2.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Laplacian smoothing can stabilize very-small-batch training under the tested LeNet recipe.

fits_no_version.finding: ResNet56 trained with smoothing for the first 40 epochs generalizes better than SGD alone despite lower training accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Early Laplacian smoothing can improve ResNet56 held-out accuracy on CIFAR-10.

fits_no_version.finding: Generator smoothing improves WGAN stability and qualitative sample quality, with smaller gains at the smaller learning rate; critic smoothing shows no clear quality improvement.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Benefits of smoothing WGAN updates depend on learning rate and whether the generator or critic is smoothed.

fits_no_version.finding: All five smoothed-RMSProp Cartpole policies exceed 1000 evaluation steps, compared with three of five ordinary-RMSProp policies.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Laplacian smoothing can improve policy evaluation outcomes in the reported Cartpole experiment.

fits_no_version.finding: On a constructed nonconvex objective, smoothed GD escapes narrow local minima where ordinary GD becomes trapped.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Laplacian smoothing can change which minima optimization reaches on constructed objectives; this does not establish a sharpness–generalization correlation.

record.problems: Several classification and sample-quality results are reported only qualitatively or in figures, without numerical test accuracies or error bars in the text. The ResNet comparison uses 25 replicas but reports histograms without summary statistics. The WGAN experiments deliberately use a large generator learning rate to accentuate instability.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label held-out accuracy under the same architecture and recipe.
Test error as width increases beyond the zero-training-error threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizers on held-out classification or language performance, including tuning and recovery conditions.
Large-batch held-out penalties under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that remove them.
Dropout's effects and its interactions with training-set size, augmentation, and weight decay.
Magnitude-scaled weight-perturbation tolerance, its association with generalization gaps, and comparison with other measures.
Accuracy effects of removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: All rows remain outside the listed versions. Their cannot_determine states denote inability to assess those versions, not uncertainty about the reported smoothing comparisons. No version-specific verdicts or missing version-bearing results are warranted.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization under the same recipe.
Width sweep beyond the zero-training-error threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD or momentum SGD under the stated tuning conditions; the paper compares RMSProp with its smoothed variant.
Large batches under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations; the paper discusses small-batch results.
Dropout effects and interactions with augmentation or weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness measurement and its correlation with train-test gaps.
Removing memorized examples and measuring resulting test accuracy.
